title: Newton's Laws of Motion

cards.h: Why does anything move at all?
cards.b:
For about 2000 years people believed, following Aristotle, that a moving object needs a continuing push. It seems obvious: stop pushing a cart and it stops.

Galileo and then Isaac Newton overturned this. In his Principia (1687), Newton set out three laws that explain the motion of falling apples, rolling carts, planets and rockets. They remain the working rules of engineering today.

cards.h: First law: things keep doing what they are doing
cards.b:
An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion keeps moving in a straight line at steady speed, unless a net force acts on it. This tendency is called inertia.

The cart stops not because motion needs a push, but because friction pushes back. On ice, with little friction, a puck slides far. In space, with none, it would slide forever.

Inertia explains why you lurch forward when a bus brakes: your body wants to keep moving.

Newton's second law

F = m a

Net force F (in newtons) equals mass m (kg) times acceleration a (m/s squared). One newton is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s squared.

Two lessons. First, the same push gives a light object more acceleration than a heavy one. Second, net matters: if you push a wall and it does not move, other forces (the wall's push back) balance yours, so the net force is zero.

cards.h: Third law: forces come in pairs
cards.b:
When body A pushes on body B, B pushes back on A with an equal and opposite force.

Swimming: you push water backward, water pushes you forward. A rocket throws hot gas down; the gas pushes the rocket up. It needs no air to push against, which is why rockets work in space.

The key point: the two forces act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other when you work out the motion of one body.

To solve any problem, draw one object and every force on it. This is a free-body diagram.

Friction opposes sliding. A good model: f = mu x N, where N is the normal force (the table's push) and mu is the friction coefficient. Rubber on dry road might have mu near 0.8; ice, near 0.05.

cards.h: Weight, mass and the normal force
cards.b:
Mass (kg) is how much matter a body has. Weight is the gravitational force on it: W = m g. A 10 kg box weighs 10 x 9.8 = 98 N on Earth.

When a box sits on a table, the table pushes up with a normal force N (normal means at right angles to the surface). Here N equals the weight, so the net vertical force is zero and the box does not accelerate.

In a lift accelerating upward, N becomes bigger than your weight, and you feel heavier. That 'feeling of weight' is really the normal force.

You push with 50 N. Friction is 20 N backwards. Vertical forces (weight and normal) cancel.

Net force = 50 - 20 = 30 N.

F = m a gives a = 30/10 = 3 m/s squared.

After 4 s from rest its speed is 12 m/s, and it has covered (1/2) x 3 x 16 = 24 m. Weight of the box: 10 x 9.8 = 98 N, so N = 98 N, and with mu = 20/98 about 0.2 for that friction.

• 'Motion needs a force.' No. Changing motion needs a force. Steady motion needs none.
  • 'Action and reaction cancel, so nothing can move.' They act on different bodies, so each body can still accelerate.
  • 'Heavy objects have more inertia only on Earth.' Inertia is mass; it is the same in space. An astronaut is just as hard to push around on the Space Station.

cards.h: From Sriharikota to the Moon's south pole
cards.b:
Every ISRO launch, from the PSLV to the LVM3 rocket that carried Chandrayaan-3, is Newton's third law at work: hot gas goes down, the rocket goes up.

Chandrayaan-3's lander Vikram touched down near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023, making India the fourth country to soft-land on the Moon. Every burn that slowed it was a calculation of F = ma, with thrust and mass changing as fuel was used.

• Objects keep their velocity unless a net force acts (inertia).
  • F = ma: net force gives acceleration, in newtons for kg and m/s squared.
  • Forces come in equal, opposite pairs on different bodies.
  • Draw a free-body diagram and add forces as vectors.

Think about it

1. Why does a coin on a card fall into the glass when you flick the card away quickly?
2. A truck and a small car collide. Which feels the larger force, and which the larger acceleration?
